solar-oven.title: Pizza box solar oven
solar-oven.blurb: Turn a pizza box into an oven that runs on sunlight, then use it to melt a s'more.
solar-oven.time: About 1 hour, plus 30 minutes of sun
materials: Pizza box (bigger works better)
Aluminum foil
Plastic wrap
Black paper
White glue and tape
Ruler and pencil
Wooden skewer or pencil to prop the lid
Graham crackers, marshmallows, chocolate
A small foil tray or pie pan
steps: Take out any cardboard liner from the pizza box.
On the lid, draw a square about one inch in from each edge.
With an adult, cut along three sides of the square with a utility knife. Leave the hinge side uncut so it makes a flap.
Cover the inside of the flap with foil, folding the edges over, and glue it smooth. This reflects sunlight into the box.
Tape plastic wrap tightly over the opening in the lid so there are no gaps. This traps the heat.
Line the bottom and inner walls of the box with foil and glue it down.
Glue black paper to the middle of the bottom. Dark colors soak up heat.
Prop the flap open at about 90 degrees with a skewer and tape.
Put a s'more on the foil tray in the middle, close the lid, and set the oven in full sun with the flap facing the sun.
Wait at least 30 minutes. Check if the marshmallow is soft. Try changing the flap angle and see if it heats faster.
solar-oven.safety: Ask an adult to do the cutting. The inside of the oven gets hot, so use an oven mitt to take food out. Works best on sunny days above 75°F.

straw-rocket.title: Straw rocket test flight
straw-rocket.blurb: Build a paper rocket that launches from a straw, then change one thing at a time to make it fly farther, like NASA engineers do.
materials: Rocket template from NASA JPL (printable PDF on the guide page)
Pencil
Scissors
Tape
Soda straw
Measuring tape or meter stick
steps: Print the rocket template and cut out the big rectangle.
Wrap the rectangle around a pencil the long way and tape it into a tube.
Cut out the two fin pieces. Tape one to the bottom of the tube so nothing sticks out past the end.
Tape the second fin piece on the opposite side to make a fin sandwich.
Bend each fin out 90 degrees so they make a plus sign when you look from below.
Twist and pinch the top of the tube around the pencil tip to make a nose cone, then tape it.
Slide the pencil out and slide a straw in.
Mark a launch line, blow hard through the straw, and measure how far the rocket flew.
Change one thing, like fin size or rocket length, and launch again. Keep a log of what helps the most.
straw-rocket.safety: Never aim a rocket at a person or animal.

scratch-catch.title: Make a catch game in Scratch
scratch-catch.blurb: Code a game where you move a character to catch falling objects and keep score. No typing code, just drag blocks.
materials: A computer or tablet with a web browser
A free Scratch account (optional, needed to save and share)
steps: Go to scratch.mit.edu and click Create.
Pick a catcher sprite, like a bowl or a cat, and move it to the bottom of the stage.
Add 'when green flag clicked' and a 'forever' loop. Inside it, make the sprite follow the mouse's x position, or move with the arrow keys.
Add a second sprite to fall from the sky, like an apple.
For the apple, use 'go to x: (pick random -220 to 220) y: 180', then 'change y by -5' inside a loop so it falls.
Make a variable called Score. When the apple is touching the catcher, add 1 to Score and send the apple back to the top.
If the apple reaches the bottom, send it back to the top without adding points.
Add a timer or a 'lives' variable so the game can end.
Click Share to post your game, and look at other people's catch games for ideas.

dance-party.title: Code a dance party
dance-party.blurb: Program dancers to move to the beat of real songs. A quick first taste of coding with blocks.
materials: A computer or tablet with a web browser
steps: Go to code.org/dance and start the activity.
Pick a song you like.
Follow the short puzzles to learn how to add dancers and set their moves.
Use 'every 2 measures' style blocks to change moves on the beat.
Add background effects that change during the song.
On the free play level, build your own routine from scratch.
Click Share to get a link to your dance party.

tinkercad-armor.title: Design armor and gear in Tinkercad
tinkercad-armor.blurb: Learn 3D design by building a shield, helmet, or sword from simple shapes, then get it ready to 3D print.
materials: A computer with a web browser
A free Tinkercad account
A 3D printer at school or a library (optional)
steps: Make a free account at tinkercad.com and start a new 3D design.
Drag a basic shape, like a cylinder, onto the workplane for the body of your shield.
Use the handles to resize it. Hold Shift to keep the proportions even.
Add more shapes for details. Turn some shapes into Holes to cut into the main shape.
Select all the pieces and press Group to combine them.
Check that nothing floats in the air, since floating parts will not print.
Export the design as an STL file.
If you can, ask a teacher or librarian to print it, or share a screenshot of your design.

sprig-game.title: Make your first game on Sprig
sprig-game.blurb: Write a tile-based game in JavaScript in your browser. Hack Club mails teens a free Sprig console when their game is accepted.
materials: A computer with a web browser
A GitHub account, to submit your game
steps: Open sprig.hackclub.com and start the tutorial in the editor.
Draw your sprites in the bitmap editor: a player, walls, and a goal.
Build your first level map with the map editor.
Use onInput to move the player with W, A, S, and D.
Set which sprites are solid so the player cannot walk through walls.
Add a win check: when the player reaches the goal, load the next level.
Add at least a few levels, plus sound or a twist that makes it yours.
Playtest it with a friend and fix anything confusing.
Follow the submission steps in the editor to send your game to the Sprig gallery on GitHub.

visual-novel.title: Write a visual novel with Ren'Py
visual-novel.blurb: Make a story game with characters, art, and choices that change the ending. Built for Hack Club's Storyboard program.
visual-novel.time: A weekend to start, then an hour a day
materials: A computer (Windows, Mac, or Linux)
Ren'Py, free from renpy.org
A drawing app for characters and backgrounds (optional)
GitHub and itch.io accounts, to publish
steps: Download Ren'Py from renpy.org and create a new project.
Plan your story on paper: the main character, the problem, and two or three endings.
Open script.rpy. Define your characters with Character(), giving each a name and color.
Write your first scene with dialogue lines.
Add backgrounds and character sprites with scene and show.
Add a menu so the player makes a choice, and use labels and jump to send each choice down a different path.
Playtest every path to make sure each ending works.
Build your game for web or desktop and upload it to itch.io.
Push your project to GitHub and submit it to Storyboard.

blot-art.title: Code art for a drawing robot
blot-art.blurb: Write JavaScript that draws generative art, then send it to Blot, Hack Club's open source pen plotter.
materials: A computer with a web browser
steps: Open the Blot editor at blot.hackclub.com.
Read through one of the beginner guides in the editor to see how drawings are made from lines.
Draw a simple shape, like a square, by listing its points.
Use a loop to repeat and rotate the shape across the page.
Add randomness so every run looks a little different.
Keep the drawing inside the page area so a plotter could draw it.
Export your art, then share it in the Blot gallery by following the guide on the site.

sine-art.title: Make music and art from sine waves
sine-art.blurb: Use code to turn math into sound and moving pictures. A fun way to see how waves work.
materials: A computer with a web browser and a code editor
steps: Follow the Oscillart jam to set up an HTML page with a canvas and a button.
Use the Web Audio API to play a tone when the button is pressed.
Draw a sine wave on the canvas that matches the tone.
Let the user type notes and change the pitch and color.
Try changing amplitude and frequency and watch how the wave changes.
Publish your page and share it.

web-os.title: Build your own web operating system
web-os.blurb: Make a desktop that runs in the browser, with draggable windows and your own mini apps.
materials: A computer with a code editor
A GitHub account, to publish with GitHub Pages
steps: Make an index.html with a desktop area and a taskbar.
Style it with CSS: wallpaper, icons, and a clock on the taskbar.
Make a window element with a title bar and a close button.
Write JavaScript so you can drag windows by their title bars.
Add apps that open in windows, like a notes app or a photo viewer.
Save notes in the browser so they stay after a refresh.
Publish your OS with GitHub Pages and share the link.

godot-platformer.title: Build a platformer in Godot
godot-platformer.blurb: Make a 2D jumping game with the free Godot engine, then publish it so friends can play in a browser.
materials: A computer
Godot 4, free from godotengine.org
Free sprite art, like the packs on kenney.nl
steps: Download Godot 4 and create a new project.
Make a player scene with a CharacterBody2D, a sprite, and a collision shape.
Attach the built-in movement script template so the player can run and jump.
Make a level with a TileMap and paint some platforms.
Add coins with Area2D nodes that disappear and add to a score when touched.
Add a camera that follows the player.
Add a goal that loads the next level.
Export to Web and upload it to itch.io.

weather-station.title: Build a weather station
weather-station.blurb: Wire a sensor to a Raspberry Pi, log temperature, humidity, and pressure, and graph the weather where you live.
materials: Raspberry Pi with power supply and SD card
BME280 sensor board
Jumper wires
Breadboard (optional)
steps: Set up Raspberry Pi OS and turn on I2C in the settings.
With the Pi off, wire the BME280: power to 3.3V, ground to ground, SDA to SDA, and SCL to SCL.
Install a Python library for the BME280 and print one reading to check it works.
Write a loop that reads temperature, humidity, and pressure every 5 minutes.
Save each reading with a timestamp to a CSV file.
Leave it running for a day, somewhere shaded outside or by a window.
Graph your data with Python and look for patterns, like when it is hottest.
Compare your readings to a local weather report.
weather-station.safety: Always unplug the Pi before changing wires.

pcb-onboard.title: Design your own PCB
pcb-onboard.blurb: Draw a circuit, lay out a real printed circuit board, and get it made. Hack Club's OnBoard program gives teens a grant to pay for manufacturing.
materials: A computer with KiCad (free)
A GitHub account
Soldering iron and parts once your board arrives
steps: Pick a small first design, like an LED badge or a business card that lights up. The Hack Club Hacker Card jam is a good starting point.
Draw the schematic in KiCad: add parts, connect them, and run the electrical rules check.
Give every part a footprint so KiCad knows its real size.
Lay out the board: place parts, draw the board outline, and route the traces.
Run the design rules check and fix every error.
Export Gerber files and upload them to JLCPCB to see the price. Take a screenshot of your cart.
Fork the hackclub/OnBoard repo and add a folder for your project with a README, cart.png, gerber.zip, your design files, and schematic.pdf.
Open a pull request and follow the checklist to apply for the grant.
When the boards arrive, solder the parts on and test them. Post photos in the #onboard channel.
pcb-onboard.safety: Soldering irons get very hot. Work in a ventilated space and wear eye protection.

hackpad.title: Build a custom macropad
hackpad.blurb: Design the PCB, 3D-printed case, and firmware for your own mini keyboard of shortcut keys. Part of Hack Club Blueprint.
materials: A computer with KiCad and a CAD program
A GitHub account
Parts from Hack Club's approved list (Seeed XIAO RP2040, switches, keycaps)
steps: Look at the example macropads in the hackclub/hackpad repo to see what a finished project includes.
Plan your layout. You get fewer than 16 inputs, like keys or knobs.
Draw the schematic in KiCad using the Seeed XIAO RP2040 as the brain.
Lay out a two-layer PCB that fits within 100 by 100 mm, and export Gerbers.
Design a 3D-printed case in CAD that fits within 200 by 200 by 100 mm.
Write firmware with QMK or KMK so each key does something useful.
Make a GitHub repo with CAD, PCB, Firmware, and production folders, plus a README with screenshots and a parts list.
Post your project in #blueprint-drafts on Hack Club Slack and submit it for design review.

genelab-data.title: Analyze real spaceflight gene data
genelab-data.blurb: Use NASA's open data to see which genes change in mice that flew in space. Real biology meets real coding.
materials: A computer with a web browser
A free Google account for Google Colab
steps: Go to NASA's Open Science Data Repository and search for a mouse spaceflight study with RNA sequencing data.
Read the study description: which tissue, how long in space, and what the control group was.
Download the differential expression table from the study's files.
Open Google Colab and load the table with pandas.
Filter for genes with an adjusted p-value under 0.05 and a large fold change.
Make a volcano plot with matplotlib, showing fold change against significance.
Pick the top 5 changed genes and look up what each one does.
Write a short summary: what changed in space, and why might that matter for astronauts?
If you like this, apply to NASA GeneLab for High Schools to go deeper.

gl4hs.title: GeneLab for High Schools
gl4hs.blurb: Learn how NASA studies what spaceflight does to living things, then analyze real omics data with bioinformatics tools in JupyterLab. Great if you like biology, computer science, or both.
gl4hs.when: Online, self-paced, about 20 hours a week from June to August. Applications have opened in mid-February and closed in mid-March.
gl4hs.req: Rising juniors and seniors, or seniors starting college in the fall. U.S. citizens or permanent residents at a U.S. high school, one biology course, and at least a 3.0 GPA.

sees.title: NASA SEES summer internship
sees.org: UT Austin Center for Space Research and NASA
sees.blurb: Work on real Earth and space science projects with NASA experts, starting online and finishing with two weeks on site in Austin.
sees.when: Online work May to July, then about two weeks in Austin in July. The application has been due in late February.
sees.req: Current sophomores and juniors who turn 16 by early July. U.S. citizens only.

nasa-ostem.title: NASA internships for graduating seniors
nasa-ostem.blurb: Paid internships at NASA centers. High school seniors can apply for the summer right after they graduate.
nasa-ostem.when: 10-week summer session. Summer 2027 applications are due March 1, 2027.
nasa-ostem.req: Must be 18 by the start date. U.S. citizens with at least a 3.0 GPA.

ssp.title: Summer Science Program
ssp.blurb: Live on a college campus and do a real research project in a small team: astrophysics, biochemistry, bacterial genomics, or cell biology.
ssp.when: About six weeks in summer. Apply during junior year and check ssp.org for this year's deadline.
ssp.req: High school juniors, ages 15 to 18. Free for families earning $75,000 or less, with discounts above that.

cosmos.title: COSMOS
cosmos.blurb: Four weeks living at a UC campus, taking college-level STEM courses. UCLA is one of the five campuses, so this one is close to home.
cosmos.when: Four weeks in summer. Applications usually open in winter.
cosmos.req: Students finishing grades 8 to 12. Financial aid is available for application and program costs.

rsi.title: Research Science Institute
rsi.org: Center for Excellence in Education at MIT
rsi.blurb: Six weeks at MIT doing your own research project with a mentor, then presenting it like a scientist. Very selective.
rsi.when: Six weeks in summer. Applications are usually due in December of junior year.
rsi.req: High school juniors. Free to attend.

mites.title: MITES Summer
mites.blurb: Six weeks of college-level math, science, and engineering classes at MIT, free of cost.
mites.when: Six weeks in summer. Applications are usually due around February 1 of junior year.
mites.req: High school juniors. Check the site for full eligibility.

cac.title: Congressional App Challenge
cac.blurb: Build any app and submit it to your member of Congress. Winners get recognized and their apps are shown in the U.S. Capitol.
cac.req: Middle and high school students. Work alone or in a team of up to four.

storyboard.title: Storyboard
storyboard.blurb: Make a visual novel and publish it on itch.io. During Storyboardtober you earn a sticker for each day you work, plus bigger prizes at the end.

sprig.title: Sprig
sprig.blurb: Make a JavaScript game in the Sprig editor. If it's accepted into the gallery, Hack Club mails you a free Sprig console to play it on.
sprig.req: Teenagers and younger get a free console. Anyone can make games.

hackclub-clubs.title: Start or join a Hack Club
hackclub-clubs.blurb: A free coding club run by students. You get workshops, events, and a big online community of teen makers.
hackclub-clubs.req: Teens. Every Hack Club program is free.

space-apps.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge
space-apps.blurb: A worldwide weekend hackathon where teams solve real challenges using NASA data.
space-apps.when: Every October. Watch for registration for the next one.
space-apps.req: Open to all ages. Students under 18 need a parent or guardian's permission.

first.title: FIRST robotics teams
first.blurb: Build and program robots on a team. FIRST LEGO League is for younger kids. FIRST Tech Challenge and FIRST Robotics Competition are for middle and high school.
first.when: Seasons start in the fall. Find a team near you on the FIRST site.

gwc.title: Girls Who Code Clubs
gwc.blurb: Free coding clubs where you learn to code by building projects that matter to you.
gwc.req: Open to girls and non-binary students. Check the site for details.

scioly.title: Science Olympiad
scioly.blurb: Team science competition with events in biology, earth science, astronomy, engineering, and building.
scioly.when: Teams form in the fall and compete in winter and spring.
scioly.req: Middle and high school teams through your school.

griffith-star.title: Free public star parties at Griffith Observatory
griffith-star.blurb: Look through telescopes on the observatory lawn with volunteer astronomers who explain what you're seeing.
griffith-star.when: Usually once a month. Check the observatory calendar for dates.
